title: Florida JEAC Opinion 2026-04
subject: A judge may not inform self-represented litigants in a family law case about a third-party software tool that assists the parties in drafting a parenting plan.
text:
ISSUE
1. May a judge inform self-represented litigants in a family law case about a third-party software tool that assists the parties in drafting a parenting plan?
ANSWER: No.

FACTS
The inquiring judge states that the software is currently being offered free of charge. The software is not court-sponsored. It was developed and is offered by a private family law attorney who practices before the family law bench in the judge’s jurisdiction. While the software is currently offered free of charge, the attorney expects the software to become a paid product in the future.
The software is an online, guided platform that helps separating parents collaboratively create a comprehensive, court-ready parenting plan by use of structured modules and AI-assisted drafting. The software includes instructional videos featuring the attorney who developed the software. The inquiring judge believes that the software could reduce the amount of judicial time spent addressing pro se parenting plan disputes.
The inquiring judge’s concern is whether referencing the software, even while it is free, could be construed as endorsing a private product or otherwise create an appearance of impropriety or partiality. The inquiring judge states that family law judges are frequently asked by self-represented litigants to suggest programs or tools but is concerned that informing litigants of the availability of such third-party resources constitutes an impermissible recommendation by a judge.

DISCUSSION
The issue presented by the inquiring judge is addressed by Canons 2A and 2B of the Code of Judicial Conduct, which state:
Canon 2
A Judge Shall Avoid Impropriety and the Appearance of Impropriety in all of the Judge's Activities
A. A judge shall respect and comply with the law and shall act at all times in a manner that promotes public confidence in the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.
B. A judge shall not allow family, social, political or other relationships to influence the judge's judicial conduct or judgment. A judge shall not lend the prestige of judicial office to advance the private interests of the judge or others; nor shall a judge convey or permit others to convey the impression that they are in a special position to influence the judge. A judge shall not testify voluntarily as a character witness.
This Committee has issued many opinions involving Canons 2A and 2B, regarding the impartiality of the judiciary and not lending the prestige of the judicial office to advance the private interests of others. See, e.g., Fla. JEAC Op. 07-21 (a judge may not be an advisory board member, with or without compensation, for an internet company which will not sell legal services or legal advice but will provide divorce information, such as, where to find a lawyer, appropriate forms at the clerk’s office, a child support calculator, online support groups and chat rooms, psychologists, and counselors); Fla. JEAC Op. 21-17 (a judge may not write comments about a book by an expert witness when the comments are intended to be included in the published book and potentially used in advertisements; Fla. JEAC Op. 25-10 (Amended) (a judge may not appear in a documentary film about high conflict family cases where the judge would speak about trends in high conflict cases in general and also his experiences witnessing the effects on children of high conflict custody disputes. The judge would not discuss any specific cases pending in any court nor would the judge accept any payment for time or reimbursement of expenses. The documentary film may possibly be shown at a location where tickets are sold, or the film itself could be sold for profit).
While the software is now free the author/attorney may in the future change that to a for-profit commercial endeavor. By informing self-represented litigants of the software program the inquiring judge could be enhancing the success of that endeavor. Even if the software remains free, it could lead to the increased business for the author/attorney. Canon 2B prohibits a judge from lending the prestige of the judicial office to advance the private interest of others.
Of further concern is that the attorney practices before the family law bench in the jurisdiction of the inquiring judge. In cases where the author/attorney appears before the bench, having his or her software promoted by a judge in that jurisdiction could cause concern to opposing attorneys or parties about impartiality.
The issue presented by the inquiring judge is also addressed by Canon 3B(10) of the Code of Judicial Conduct, which states:
Canon 3
A Judge Shall Perform the Duties of Judicial Office Impartially and Diligently
B. Adjudicative Responsibilities.
(10) A judge shall not, with respect to parties or classes of parties, cases, controversies or issues likely to come before the court, make pledges, promises or commitments that are inconsistent with the impartial performance of the adjudicative duties of the office.
If the recommendation by the inquiring judge to use the software program is followed and used by a party or parties who then suffer an adverse ruling this could be problematic to the judge. Pro se litigants may well expect that plans drafted using the software would be approved by the judge and would be upset if the judge denied a plan drafted using the software recommended or mentioned by that same judge. Further, “endorsing” a particular software could be perceived as running counter to the prohibition in Canon 3B(10) of making any “commitment” on how the judge would rule in any case or type of case. As noted, pro se parties and attorneys might see the mere mention of the software as an endorsement which commits the judge to grant those plans drafted with the software.
The Committee finds that the inquiring judge should decline to recommend or mention the software because:
a) Informing litigants of the existence of the software lends the prestige of the judicial office to the attorney and advances the private interest of the attorney;
b) Doing so could cause concerns about impartiality; and,
Parties and attorneys might see it as an endorsement which commits the judge to grant those plans drafted with the software.

REFERENCES
Fla. Code Jud. Conduct, Canon 2A and 2B, Canon 3B(10)
Fla. JEAC Op. 2007-21, 2021-17, 2025-10

SUBJECT
A judge may not inform self-represented litigants in a family law case about a third-party software tool that assists the parties in drafting a parenting plan.
